summary.text: Writing the factors in terms of \(U=1+x\), \(V=y+z\), and \(W=y-z\), the proof expands by degree and uses \(W^2=V^2-4yz\) with binomial recurrences to establish \(\binom{2n}{2j}[y^nz^n]V^{2n-2j}W^{2j}=(-1)^j\binom{2n}{n}\binom nj\). Substitution reduces the desired coefficient to products of central binomial coefficients and \(\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj^2\), which equals \(\binom{2n}{n}\) by Vandermonde’s identity.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F_n(x,y,z)=(1+x+y+z)^{2n}(1+x+y-z)^n(1+x-y+z)^n.
\]
We prove, for every integer \(n\ge 0\), that
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]F_n(x,y,z)=\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
All polynomials below have integer coefficients, and \([x^ay^bz^c]\) denotes coefficient extraction.

Set
\[
U=1+x,\qquad V=y+z,\qquad W=y-z.
\]
Then
\[
1+x+y+z=U+V,
\]
while
\[
1+x+y-z=U+W,\qquad 1+x-y+z=U-W.
\]
Consequently,
\[
F_n=(U+V)^{2n}(U+W)^n(U-W)^n
     =(U+V)^{2n}(U^2-W^2)^n.
\]
The last equality follows from \((U+W)(U-W)=U^2-W^2\), followed by taking the \(n\)-th power.

Expand both factors by the binomial theorem:
\[
(U+V)^{2n}
 =\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{2n}{k}U^{2n-k}V^k
\]
and
\[
(U^2-W^2)^n
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^j\binom nj U^{2(n-j)}W^{2j}.
\]
Multiplying gives
\[
F_n=
\sum_{j=0}^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{2n}
(-1)^j\binom{2n}{k}\binom nj
U^{4n-k-2j}V^kW^{2j}.
\tag{1}
\]

Here \(U\) depends only on \(x\), whereas \(V\) and \(W\) depend only on \(y,z\). Moreover, \(V^kW^{2j}\) is homogeneous of total \((y,z)\)-degree \(k+2j\). A term in (1) can therefore contain \(y^nz^n\), whose total \((y,z)\)-degree is \(2n\), only if
\[
k+2j=2n.
\]
For \(0\le j\le n\), this forces
\[
k=2n-2j,
\]
which indeed lies between \(0\) and \(2n\). For this value of \(k\), the exponent of \(U\) is
\[
4n-k-2j=4n-(2n-2j)-2j=2n.
\]
Thus every potentially contributing term contains \(U^{2n}=(1+x)^{2n}\), and
\[
[x^n]U^{2n}=\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
It follows that
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]F_n
=\binom{2n}{n}\,S_n,
\tag{2}
\]
where
\[
S_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^j\binom nj
\binom{2n}{2n-2j}\,c_{n,j}
\tag{3}
\]
and
\[
c_{n,j}=[y^nz^n](y+z)^{2n-2j}(y-z)^{2j}.
\tag{4}
\]
We now evaluate the weighted coefficients appearing in (3).

For \(0\le j\le n\), the polynomial in (4) is homogeneous of total degree \(2n\). Setting \(y=t\) and \(z=1\), the coefficient of \(y^nz^n\) becomes the coefficient of \(t^n\). Since \(2j\) is even,
\[
(t-1)^{2j}=(1-t)^{2j}.
\]
Hence
\[
c_{n,j}=[t^n](1+t)^{2n-2j}(1-t)^{2j}.
\tag{5}
\]

We claim the following key identity:
\[
\boxed{\binom{2n}{2j}c_{n,j}
=(-1)^j\binom{2n}{n}\binom nj}
\qquad(0\le j\le n).
\tag{6}
\]
To prove it, introduce a second indeterminate \(u\) and consider
\[
Q(t,u)=\bigl((1+t)+u(1-t)\bigr)^{2n}.
\]
We compute \([t^nu^{2j}]Q(t,u)\) in two orders.

First expand with respect to \(u\). Choosing the term \(u(1-t)\) exactly \(2j\) times gives
\[
[u^{2j}]Q(t,u)
=\binom{2n}{2j}(1+t)^{2n-2j}(1-t)^{2j}.
\]
Using (5), extraction of \(t^n\) therefore yields
\[
[t^nu^{2j}]Q(t,u)=\binom{2n}{2j}c_{n,j}.
\tag{7}
\]

On the other hand, rearrange the expression inside the power as
\[
(1+t)+u(1-t)=(1+u)+(1-u)t.
\]
Now extract the coefficient of \(t^n\) first. In the \(2n\)-th power, one must choose \((1-u)t\) exactly \(n\) times and \(1+u\) the remaining \(n\) times. Thus
\[
[t^n]Q(t,u)
=\binom{2n}{n}(1+u)^n(1-u)^n
=\binom{2n}{n}(1-u^2)^n.
\]
By the binomial theorem,
\[
(1-u^2)^n=\sum_{r=0}^{n}(-1)^r\binom nr u^{2r}.
\]
Therefore
\[
[t^nu^{2j}]Q(t,u)
=(-1)^j\binom{2n}{n}\binom nj.
\tag{8}
\]
Equating (7) and (8) proves (6). Notice that this argument involves no division, so it also covers the endpoint values \(j=0,j=n\) and the case \(n=0\).

Return to the sum \(S_n\). For \(0\le j\le n\), binomial symmetry gives
\[
\binom{2n}{2n-2j}=\binom{2n}{2j}.
\]
Combining this with (6), the \(j\)-th summand in (3) becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
(-1)^j\binom nj\binom{2n}{2n-2j}c_{n,j}
&=(-1)^j\binom nj\binom{2n}{2j}c_{n,j}\\
&=(-1)^j\binom nj
   \left((-1)^j\binom{2n}{n}\binom nj\right)\\
&=\binom{2n}{n}\binom nj^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \((-1)^{2j}=1\). Hence
\[
S_n=\binom{2n}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj^2.
\tag{9}
\]

It remains to use the central case of Vandermonde’s identity:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj^2=\binom{2n}{n}.
\tag{10}
\]
For completeness, (10) follows by taking the coefficient of \(t^n\) in
\[
(1+t)^n(1+t)^n=(1+t)^{2n}.
\]
The coefficient on the right is \(\binom{2n}{n}\). On the left, the product rule for coefficients gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj\binom n{n-j},
\]
and \(\binom n{n-j}=\binom nj\), yielding (10).

Substituting (10) into (9) gives
\[
S_n=\binom{2n}{n}^2.
\]
Finally, (2) now yields
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]F_n
=\binom{2n}{n}\binom{2n}{n}^2
=\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
For \(n=0\), the same formulas say that the coefficient of \(1\) in the constant polynomial \(1\) is \(1=\binom00^3\), so the statement holds for all \(n\ge0\). Thus the coefficient in the conjecture is exactly the sequence term \(a(n)=\binom{2n}{n}^3\).
